item.title: Your Setlist Shouldn't Survive the Audience
item.author: Devin Frank
item.description: Why the best live setlists change with the room. Devin Frank shares lessons on requests, reading the audience, building a flexible repertoire, and making every show worth coming back to.
item.content:encoded:
Live music is expensive. That is not a criticism of musicians. We should be paid fairly for what we do. But from the venue side, live music is an investment—and increasingly, venues have to think carefully about whether that investment makes sense.

In my first Field Note, I talked about some of the things we can do as musicians to make ourselves valuable to the places that hire us: promote the show, arrive prepared, start on time, pay attention to breaks, provide venues with good promotional material, and understand that the success of the night matters. But there's another part of that equation: the show itself.

Put Yourself in the Audience

Imagine you're a customer at a local bar or restaurant. Over six months, you happen to catch the same musician three times. The first time, you enjoy it. The second time, you start recognizing some of the songs. But by the third time, you realize something: it's the same show. Same songs. Same order. Same stories. Same jokes. You already know what's coming next. How engaged are you by that third show?

More importantly, when you're deciding where to go next month and you see that musician's name again, you might think: "I've already seen them." That's a problem—not just for the musician, but for the venue too.

Now Change 10 or 15 Songs

Let's run the same scenario again, except this time each show is a little different. Maybe 10 or 15 songs change between performances. Maybe they take requests. Maybe on your third visit, they pull out a song you love that you haven't heard before. Suddenly your reaction changes. "I wonder what they'll do this time." That's the difference.

A Setlist Is a Plan, Not a Contract

A setlist gives you somewhere to start. But I don't think it should lock you into where the night goes, because you don't really know what kind of show you're playing until you meet the audience. Maybe you expected a younger crowd and the room ends up mostly 50+. Maybe people are responding well to country. Maybe they're singing along to every upbeat song. Follow that energy. The audience is constantly giving you information. The trick is being willing to listen to it.

Sometimes the Audience Writes the Setlist

My duo has a QR code we put out at shows. Audience members can see our available songs and send requests. One night, requests just kept coming. Before long, almost the entire show had become requests. The audience was writing the setlist in real time. Requests are data. If an entire room starts requesting songs, they're telling you what kind of show they want. Give it to them.

Sometimes One Song Changes the Room

We've seen this happen with Piano Man. People see piano and expect quiet background music. But then you play Piano Man. People recognize it. They start singing. The energy changes. If one song completely changes how the room responds, maybe that's where your show goes next.

But How Do You Have Enough Songs?

My duo has a repertoire of more than 350 songs. Having a large repertoire means we have options. If the crowd skews older, we lean into older material. If people want country, we go further in that direction. If requests start pouring in, there's enough variety for the audience to shape the show. You don't need 350 songs to start. Add one new song a month and you've added 12 by next year.

You're a Cover Band, Not a Tribute Band

This mental hurdle holds musicians back. If you're playing covers, you're covering the song—you're not necessarily reproducing it. Those are different things. Does your strumming pattern have to match exactly? No. Does the audience care about the exact voicing? Probably not. Is the original key uncomfortable for your voice? Change it. The goal is to respect the song and keep what makes people recognize it. After that, make it yours.

Your Audience Probably Isn't Grading You

Musicians hear things differently. We notice every mistake. Most people aren't deciding if you're perfect. They're deciding: am I enjoying this? Do I recognize the song? Can I sing along? Does this feel good? That's the test. I'd rather play a simplified version of a song the room is excited to hear than refuse to play it because I haven't perfected every detail.

Give Them a Reason to Come Back

You don't control how often they go out or which venue they choose. But you can control what happens when they see you. If they've seen you before, give them something different. Change some songs. Take requests. Follow the room. The point is creating enough flexibility that your show responds to the people who are actually there. Because I don't want someone thinking "I've already seen that show." I want them thinking: "I've seen them before. I wonder what they'll do this time."

Field Note: A setlist is a tool, not a script. Plan enough to walk in prepared. Then pay attention to the people in front of you. Their requests, reactions, and energy are telling you something. Be willing to change the plan.

You don't have to perfectly recreate recordings. Learn the song. Respect what makes it recognizable. Put your own spin on it. Because a setlist gives you where to start. Your audience tells you where to go.

item.title: What Venues Actually Want From Musicians
item.author: Devin Frank
item.description: I've stood on both sides of the stage—as a musician, sound engineer, venue owner, and customer. Here's what every working musician should know about what venues actually want.
item.content:encoded:
After 15 years away from music, a series of events led me not only back into performing, but back into it in ways I never imagined. Today, I perform throughout Northwest Ohio as part of a cover duo. On any given month, we might play a retirement community, a church service, a golf club, a winery, a restaurant patio, a county fair, a wedding, or a neighborhood bar.

But performing is only one piece of what I do. I also run front-of-house sound for everyone from solo musicians to six-piece bands. My family's business owns a wine café where I book musicians and often run sound there as well. On top of that, another one of my businesses regularly puts me in venues where I experience local music simply as a customer.

That combination has given me a perspective I never expected: I've been the musician hoping the venue appreciates my work. I've been the sound engineer trying to make everyone on stage happy. I've been the venue wondering whether live music is helping or hurting the night's business. And I've been the customer who just wanted to enjoy dinner without shouting across the table.

Remember What the Venue Is Buying

When a venue hires live music, it isn't simply buying three hours of entertainment. It's making a business decision. If a venue pays me $200 to perform and feeds me dinner afterward, that isn't just a paycheck. It's an investment the venue hopes will improve the entire evening. Once you start looking at it that way, your job becomes much bigger than simply playing the right notes.

Promotion Is Part of the Job

Share the event. Mention the venue. Post photos afterward. Tag the business. Thank them publicly. Those things take only a few minutes, but they tell the venue something important: "This musician wants this night to succeed just as much as we do." Talent might get you booked the first time. Being a partner is what gets you invited back.

Show Up Ready

Being on time doesn't mean walking through the door ten minutes before your start time. It means arriving early enough to unload, set up calmly, troubleshoot problems, sound check, greet the staff, and still be ready to begin exactly when you're scheduled.

Don't Let the Clock Tell You When to Take a Break

Sometimes reading the room is more important than following your routine. If you're scheduled to play until 9:00 but the room is packed and engaged, keep playing. If it's empty, adjusting might be better for everyone. The venues I've worked with notice those moments.

Give the Venue Something Worth Promoting

Help the venue promote you. You don't need an expensive photographer. Most modern smartphones take incredible photos. Find good lighting. Wear what you'd normally wear on stage. Take twenty pictures. Pick the best three. Now every venue that books you has quality images they can use.

Remember Why You Were Hired

The venue didn't hire you because they wanted background music. They hired you because they believed you could make the entire evening better. Every decision you make—from how you promote the show, to when you take a break, to how you interact with customers and staff—either increases or decreases that value.

Field Note: The best musicians aren't always the ones with the biggest song list or the fastest guitar solos. They're the ones who make the entire night more successful—for the audience, the staff, and the venue.

Being a great musician might get you booked once. Being someone who helps the venue succeed is what gets you invited back.
